candidates.label: A
candidates.abstract: Choosing an accelerator dataflow requires reasoning about computation placement, tensor reuse, buffering, and communication together. A stationary-data label leaves too much of that mapping unspecified to explain when reuse becomes useful performance. We present MAESTRO, an analytical exploration tool that expresses dataflow with TemporalMap, SpatialMap, and Cluster directives. From workload, mapping, and hardware inputs, MAESTRO derives temporal reuse, spatial reuse, and communication opportunities at each hierarchy level, then estimates runtime, activity counts, energy, buffer requirements, and utilization. Reuse depends on supporting multicast, reduction, bandwidth, and buffers; energy estimates combine activity counts with component costs. Runtime validation against a 64-PE MAERI RTL simulation on VGG16 and reported Eyeriss runtimes on AlexNet yields average absolute error within 3.9% for those comparisons. A modeled study of five dataflow styles on operators from five DNN models finds that preferred mappings vary by operator, with adaptive choices showing potential runtime and energy reductions of 37% and 10%. MAESTRO also explores hardware configurations under area and power constraints, pruning infeasible regions with cost lower bounds. One KC-P/VGG16-CONV2 search explores 3,936,256 points in 12.20 minutes, identifying 175,861 valid points without fully simulating every explored point. These results establish a validated analytical capability within the tested scope, not a universal error bound or measured chip improvement.
introduction: An accelerator's dataflow determines when tensor computations execute and where they are placed across processing elements. Those choices interact with layer dimensions, available parallelism, data reuse, buffer capacity, and communication bandwidth. A stationary-data label describes only part of this mapping: it does not fully specify how tensor elements move through a hierarchy or whether the machine can exploit the reuse that the schedule exposes. Spatial reuse needs appropriate communication support, such as multicast or reduction, while temporal reuse needs suitable storage. Adding PEs or buffers can therefore leave a bandwidth constraint unresolved. The design question is how to connect an explicit mapping to its resource demands and resulting behavior, so that comparisons explain the interaction between a dataflow and its supporting hardware.

MAESTRO makes that connection through an analytical representation of dataflow. TemporalMap and SpatialMap specify mapping in time and space, and Cluster expresses hierarchy. Given the workload, mapping, and hardware, the analysis derives tensor reuse and communication opportunities at each hierarchy level and estimates runtime, activity counts, energy, buffer requirements, and utilization. It conditions exploitable reuse on the available buffers and communication mechanisms, including NoC bandwidth, multicast, and reductions. Energy follows from the estimated activities and component energy costs; hardware exploration additionally uses synthesized component area and power costs. This representation supports examining different dataflow styles while abstracting implementation differences. It also enables a search over PE count, local buffers, shared buffers, and NoC bandwidth under area and power constraints, using cost lower bounds to skip infeasible regions. MAESTRO's delivered capability is analytical exploration; automatic dataflow tuning and RTL generation remain future plans.

We validate runtime predictions against a 64-PE MAERI RTL simulation [kwon2018maeri] on VGG16 and reported Eyeriss runtimes on AlexNet. Average absolute runtime error is within 3.9% for those comparisons, without establishing a universal prediction bound or measured energy-error result. In a modeled case study of five dataflow styles on operators from five DNN models, preferred mappings change with operator characteristics; adaptive choices show potential runtime and energy reductions of 37% and 10%. Hardware exploration uses an Intel i7-8700K host with 32 GB memory, synthesized 28 nm building-block costs, and constraints of 16 mm² and 450 mW. These are search settings, not hardware overhead for MAESTRO. For KC-P on VGG16-CONV2, Figure13(c) reports 3,936,256 explored points, 175,861 valid points, and 12.20 minutes; lower-bound pruning means the explored count is not a count of full simulations. The evidence thus supports a practical way to analyze mapping and hardware interactions within the validated cases, while the dataflow results remain modeled comparisons rather than proof that one manufactured accelerator is superior.

candidates.label: B
candidates.abstract: Choosing a DNN accelerator dataflow requires reasoning about scheduling, placement, reuse, and the hardware that can support them. A stationary-data label cannot capture how layer dimensions interact with buffering, communication bandwidth, and parallelism. MAESTRO makes these relationships explicit through TemporalMap, SpatialMap, and Cluster directives. From workload, mapping, and hardware inputs, its analytical model derives reuse and communication opportunities at each hierarchy level and estimates runtime, activity counts, energy, buffer requirements, and utilization. Opportunities become useful only when multicast, reductions, buffers, and bandwidth provide the required support. Runtime validation against a 64-PE MAERI RTL simulation on VGG16 and reported Eyeriss runtimes on AlexNet yields average absolute error within 3.9% for those comparisons. A modeled study of five dataflow styles across operators from five DNN models finds potential runtime and energy reductions of 37% and 10% through adaptive choices. Hardware exploration varies PE count, buffers, and NoC bandwidth under area and power constraints, skipping infeasible regions through cost lower bounds. One KC-P/VGG16-CONV2 search reports 3,936,256 explored points, 175,861 valid points, and 12.20 minutes; explored points are not full simulations. MAESTRO thus supports analytical comparison of mappings and hardware configurations. The validation does not establish universal prediction accuracy or measured energy accuracy, and automatic dataflow tuning and RTL generation remain future work.
introduction: A DNN accelerator's dataflow specifies when tensor computations execute and where they are placed. That decision determines opportunities for spatial reuse and temporal reuse, but their value depends on the operator dimensions and the supporting machine. A mapping that exposes multicast or reduction opportunities cannot realize them without suitable communication hardware, just as reuse cannot compensate for an unsuitable buffer capacity. More PEs or more buffering alone may therefore leave a bandwidth-constrained design unimproved. These interactions make stationary-data labels insufficient for comparing complete mappings. In the broader setting of systematic accelerator evaluation [parashar2019timeloop], the challenge addressed here is to express a mapping precisely enough to connect its reuse opportunities to runtime and resource requirements.

MAESTRO represents dataflow with TemporalMap, SpatialMap, and Cluster directives. Given a workload, mapping, and hardware configuration, the analysis derives tensor reuse and communication opportunities at each hierarchy level. It then estimates runtime, activity counts, energy, buffer requirements, and utilization, connecting placement and scheduling choices to the resources that sustain them. Energy estimates combine activity counts with component energy estimates; design-space experiments also use synthesized component area and power costs. The same framework explores PE count, local and shared buffer capacity, and NoC bandwidth under area and power constraints. Cost lower bounds allow the search to skip infeasible regions. This enables comparison of interdependent hardware choices without equating every explored point with a full simulation, or treating abstract dataflow comparisons as measurements of manufactured accelerators.

We validate runtime predictions against a 64-PE MAERI RTL simulation on VGG16 and reported Eyeriss runtimes on AlexNet. Average absolute runtime error is within 3.9% for these comparisons, which neither establishes a bound across all dataflows nor validates energy error. A modeled comparison of five dataflow styles on operators from five DNN models shows that preferred mappings change with operator characteristics; adaptive choices offer potential runtime and energy reductions of 37% and 10% in that case study. Hardware search experiments use an Intel i7-8700K with 32 GB memory, synthesized 28 nm component costs, and constraints of 16 mm² and 450 mW. In the KC-P/VGG16-CONV2 run, the search explores 3,936,256 points, identifies 175,861 valid points, and takes 12.20 minutes. Those constraints describe the searched hardware, not overhead imposed by MAESTRO. The demonstrated contribution is an analytical exploration tool; automatic dataflow tuning and RTL generation remain future capabilities.
